content:
Suez Canal revenue rose 42% in July from the year earlier, as the Iran war's effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz and Houthi threats in the southern Red Sea led more ships to use the Egyptian waterway.

A total of 1 340 vessels transited the canal that month, according to data from state statistics agency CAPMAS. That's 27% more than in July 2025 and compares with 1 208 ships this June, extending a partial recovery that began earlier in the year.

Oil tankers accounted for 526 of July's vessels, versus 485 the month before.

The increase likely at least partly reflects the rerouting of Saudi Arabian oil exports via the Red Sea due to the shuttering of Hormuz. A subsequent threat from Yemen's Houthi rebels has spurred many ships to exit north rather than cross the Bab El-Mandeb, another chokepoint.

Canal income rose to $505 million in July, CAPMAS data showed, the highest monthly level since December 2023. Traffic volumes plunged in early 2024 when the Houthis began targeting international shipping in the southern Red Sea to pressure Israel during its war against Hamas in Gaza.

The waterway that's the shortest sea route between Europe and Asia has, along with tourism and overseas remittances, traditionally been a key source of foreign exchange for Egypt.

The Suez Canal Authority expects full-year revenue to climb to between $5.8 billion and $6 billion from $4.1 billion in 2025, Chairman Osama Rabie told a local TV talk show last week.

Despite the recent uptick, both crossings and revenue remain far below their pre-Gaza war levels. The waterway brought in a record $10.2 billion in 2023 and some 2 300 ships crossed in April of that year, according to CAPMAS data.

The resurgence is expected to continue in the coming months, with both the rerouting of Asia-bound oil exports and a number of European shippers announcing the resumption of some of their Red Sea services, said Mohamed Abu Basha, head of macroeconomic analysis at investment bank EFG Hermes.
title: Suez Canal revival gathers pace as Hormuz crisis reroutes ships

Adidas has apologized for "offense" caused by an Israeli campaign featuring wounded IDF veteran Shalev Biton, after pro-Palestinian activists launched boycott calls over his participation in a promotion for the company's Single Shoe service.

"We recognize that an image used in a recent local activation by the local team has raised concerns and strong reactions. It was never our intent to cause offense and we apologize for anyone affected," Adidas said in a statement from its global headquarters. "We acknowledge the concerns that have been raised and are taking the feedback seriously."

The company added that it has a "long-standing commitment" to communities across the Middle East and said it would "continue to listen, learn and work to ensure that our actions reflect the inclusive values we stand for."

The apology followed several days of backlash over Biton's appearance in the Israeli campaign. Biton, an amputee runner, was among a group of disabled athletes promoting Adidas' Single Shoe service, which allows customers who need only one shoe to purchase a single shoe rather than a pair.

Boycott calls spread rapidly on social media, with some posts drawing millions of views. Several accounts accused Adidas of featuring an Israeli soldier who had lost his leg while fighting in Gaza during the current war.

Biton, however, lost his leg in 2021, not during the current Gaza war.

He served as a combat soldier in Battalion 931 of the IDF's Nahal Brigade and was seriously wounded on May 12, 2021, during Operation Guardian of the Walls, when an anti-tank missile fired from Gaza struck a military vehicle on the Israeli side of the border. Staff Sgt. Omer Tabib was killed in the attack.

After several surgeries, Biton's left leg was amputated. He later underwent rehabilitation and returned to running with a prosthetic limb.

Biton announced his collaboration with Adidas on Instagram on August 26, saying that after returning to running he repeatedly had to buy full pairs of shoes despite using only one. He described the arrival of Single Shoe in Israel as part of a broader effort to make sports more accessible to people with disabilities.

One of the most widely circulated posts against the campaign came from the Land Palestine account on X and drew nearly 4 million views. Other activists circulated images comparing Biton with Palestinian children who lost limbs in Gaza and accused Adidas of ignoring Palestinian amputees.

Before issuing its apology, Adidas stressed that Single Shoe was a global accessibility initiative and had not been developed specifically for Israeli soldiers.

The company said the service launched in Europe in January 2026 and was developed with communities and professional organizations, including the British Paralympic Association.

"We are aware that interpretations in recent days have misrepresented the purpose of the service," Adidas said in its earlier response. "It is important to clarify that this is a global initiative in
title: Adidas apologizes after boycott calls over campaign featuring wounded IDF veteran

A protester holds a sign reading ''Resist apartheid, genocide, occupation, ethnic cleansing, and settler terrorism'' during a demonstration against the ongoing war and starvation in Gaza, attended by thousands of Jews and Palestinians, at Habima Square in Tel Aviv, Israel.

London - Britain's government was set Tuesday to announce sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, a minister indicated, in a move likely to anger Israel and the United States.

The decision would signal a toughening of the UK's stance on Israel under new Labour Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who entered Downing Street in July after Keir Starmer stepped down.

It comes following weeks of increasing attacks by Israeli settlers against Palestinian villages in the occupied territory that some western governments fear threatens the two-state solution.

Government minister Pat McFadden said Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband would make a statement to parliament laying out "measures specifically targeted at the expansion of these settlements, which are illegal under international law in the West Bank".

He told Sky News that the changes, on which he provided no further detail, would be motivated by "the idea of keeping alive this possibility of seeing a Palestinian state alongside Israel".

"I think it's also important to say that Israel is an important trading partner for the UK. This isn't intended to be a boycott of all Israeli goods."

UK government ministers have suggested recently that goods coming out of the illegal settlements could be subject to trade restrictions as part of the changes.

Miliband, son of Jewish refugees to Britain, vowed last Tuesday to announce a "comprehensive" reset of policy towards Israel and condemned "appalling settler terrorism" in the occupied West Bank.

Miliband called the so-called E1 development plan for more than 1,200 homes greenlighted by Israel last year "the crossing of a red line, as it cuts through the heart of the West Bank and risks making a Palestinian state unviable".

Rare condemnation from Netanyahu

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has vowed to keep establishing the settlements despite mounting international pressure, promising a major wave of immigration to the Palestinian territory.

Some of the violence by settlers in recent weeks had drawn rare condemnation from Netanyahu and unusually strong criticism from the US ambassador, as well as more typical critics in European capitals.

In September last year, Starmer announced that Britain was formally recognising a Palestinian state, marking a historic shift in decades of British foreign policy.

According to an AFP tally based on data from the Palestinian health ministry, Israeli forces or settlers have killed at least 1,105 Palestinians in the West Bank, including both militants and civilians, since the start of the Gaza war in October 2023.

More than 500,000 Israelis live in illegal settlements in the Palestinian territory, among some three million Palesti

Israeli soldiers accused of atrocities were welcomed into the Sydney Marathon under the extraordinary guise of a 'peace delegation', writes Max Gross.

AUSTRALIA'S ANNUAL 42-kilometre Sydney Marathon was held on Sunday 30 August and involved more than 40,000 runners from more than 40 countries.

One of those countries was Israel and, as reported by Michael West, included:

As many as 40 former and current IDF soldiers and associates ... sponsored by AIJAC and the Zionist Council of NSW...

...Australian Chris Sidoti, UN Human Rights Investigator, has called for Israeli military personnel who have served in Gaza to be interrogated for war crimes.

NSW court draws a line between criticism of Israel and antisemitism

A landmark NSW Supreme Court ruling challenges attempts to conflate criticism of Israel with antisemitism.

The annual charity event hoped to raise $13 million. Last year, it raised a record-breaking $8 million, and a total of more than $36 million since its launch in 2000 -- the money dispersed to genuinely worthy and needful causes.

So it's pretty disturbing that among those 'former and current IDF soldiers' are members of Israel's notorious Golani Brigade.

The Golani Brigade is linked to an attack on two ambulance convoys in Rafah, Gaza, where the bodies of murdered victims were buried in a mass grave, in March last year.

The Zionist lobby possibly invited these alleged war criminals to participate in the marathon to provoke an outraged public response that may then be labelled as "antisemitism".

But opposing Israel, opposing genocide and supporting Palestinian sovereignty, statehood and rights to self-defence and existence, is not antisemitism.

To be absolutely clear, the NSW Supreme Court has ruled that criticism of Israel does not breach the law, concluding that it is not antisemitic to criticise Israel.

The Australian Government could have and should have revoked the entry visas of those IDF soldiers. The marathon organisers could have and should have banned those Israeli soldiers from participating.

Despite online criticism and protests, the IDF soldiers participated in the prestigious race.

Meanwhile, Chris Minns, the Premier of my home state of New South Wales (NSW), used the Dural "antisemitism terrorism" hoax to rush draconian anti-protest legislation through Parliament in an attempt to outlaw public demonstrations against Israel.

Jillian Segal's 'Understanding Antisemitism in Australia': Putting Israel beyond criticism

Dr Evan Jones examines how Jillian Segal's antisemitism framework conflates criticism of Israel with antisemitism and threatens legitimate public debate.

Minns has also ordered police to attack people objecting to the morally and ethically grotesque state reception given to Israeli President Isaac Herzog, a genocide advocate.

He also proposes to arm Jewish-only "security guards" -- a move opposed even by the NSW Police. The NSW Police that used Israeli spyware, Cellebrite, more than 30,000 times s

Military raids, attacks on Palestinians and Lebanese children come as emigration rises and election divisions deepen.

Israel faced mounting political, social and international pressure on Monday as its forces continued operations in the occupied Palestinian territories and Lebanon, while new figures showed declining returns of Israelis from abroad and deepening divisions ahead of October's general election.

The developments came as Israeli authorities imposed a curfew during a military raid near occupied East Jerusalem, Palestinian rights groups reported a wave of disciplinary action against students criticizing the Gaza war, and Palestinian amputees condemned an Adidas campaign featuring a former Israeli soldier.

Meanwhile, Israeli parliamentary data showed a sharp decline in the number of citizens returning from abroad, while a new opinion poll put former army chief Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party ahead of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud.

Curfew imposed near East Jerusalem

Israeli military vehicles and bulldozers entered Shuafat refugee camp and the nearby town of Anata near occupied East Jerusalem on Monday amid a heavy troop deployment, according to the Jerusalem Governorate.

The army announced a curfew over loudspeakers and later said it had launched what it described as a "focused" operation targeting alleged terrorist activity and infrastructure. It did not provide evidence for the claims or specify how long the operation would last.

Elsewhere in the occupied West Bank, Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians and damaged property in several areas, according to Palestinian officials, local witnesses and WAFA news agency.

In the Ramallah area, settlers entered Burqa and moved through its streets, while others erected a tent on Mount Al-Qarana near Deir Abu Mashal. Settlers also moved timber toward illegal outposts west of Al-Mughayyir.

Near Hebron, a settler attacked a Palestinian woman's vehicle and smashed its windows, according to Voice of Palestine radio.

South of Yatta, settlers re-established an illegal outpost in Wadi al-Rakhim hours after Israeli forces had dismantled it, local activist Osama Makhamra told Anadolu. Israeli forces also raided Khirbet Imneizil, entered a Palestinian home and damaged property, he said.

In Salfit, Israeli settlers continued clearing Palestinian land northwest of Deir Ballut for an 11th consecutive day.

Palestinian authorities say Israeli settlers carried out 3,488 attacks across the occupied West Bank during the first half of 2026.

Gaza amputees condemn Adidas campaign

In Gaza, Palestinians who lost limbs during Israeli attacks have criticized Adidas over a local campaign featuring former Israeli soldier Shalev Biton, who lost a leg and appeared in a promotion for the company's Single Shoe service.

The service provides footwear options for people who need only one shoe, including some amputees.

Palestinian amputees said the campaign highlighted a stark disparity between access to pr
title: Israel faces mounting pressure at home and abroad

In politics, timing often carries a clearer message than the event itself. The meeting between Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi in El Alamein on Tuesday is significant not so much for what transpired during the meeting, but for its timing. The meeting cannot be understood in isolation from recent events: the growing tension between Athens and Ankara over the Aegean Sea, the signing of the $3.5 billion Achilles' Shield defense deal with Israel, the increasing defense cooperation between Egypt and Turkey, and the escalating tensions between Turkey and Israel in Syria.

Achilles' Shield deal

Greece recently signed the $3.5 billion Achilles' Shield deal with Israel, positioning Athens as Israel's closest security ally in the Eastern Mediterranean, at a time when relations between Israel and Egypt have been strained since the Gaza war.

Mitsotakis' swift visit to Egypt followed, could serve as an attempt to reassure Cairo that the Greek alliance with Tel Aviv did not imply bias against Egypt, and as a message to Ankara that relations between Cairo and Athens were excellent. For his part, Greek Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis expressed this clearly when he described Egypt as a "primary target" for Greece diplomatically, and characterized his relationship with his Egyptian counterpart, Badr Abdelatty, as "fraternal."

In this sense, the Cairo visit falls within the same logic: establishing a diplomatic line with Egypt at the very moment Athens finalized the arms deal with Israel is not a coincidence, but rather two complementary steps in a single strategy.

The Achilles' Shield deal was not merely a military decision, but a political one made at the highest level. Defense Minister Nikos Dendias described it as "an indispensable response to geopolitical challenges, transforming Greek defense from a simple weapons system into a comprehensive deterrent." This reveals that the deal was designed as a strategic message to Ankara, not a routine armament acquisition. Meanwhile, Athens simultaneously raised the issue of Turkish provocations in the Aegean Sea at the European level.

The ideological background to this tension is well-known: Turkey' "Blue Homeland" doctrine, which considers the entire Eastern Mediterranean a sphere of Turkish influence, is reinforced by Turkey's construction of over 50 warships, some of which are aimed at countries like Pakistan and Saudi Arabia - Turkey's partners in the Mecca Agreement, which Egypt, is hesitant to join.

Egypt and Turkey

In recent months, relations between Egypt and Turkey have appeared to be growing closer, as evidenced by diplomatic visits and defense cooperation deals. However, it is no secret that current Egyptian-Turkish relations are "conditional." The two sides have drawn closer for geopolitical reasons, including their stance on Israel and the desire to reduce their reliance on American arms.

In politics, this rapprochement, built on temporary in
title: Timing is everything in the Egypt-Greece relationship

James Sinkinson is the president of Facts and Logic About the Middle East (FLAME), an organization dedicated to researching Middle East developments and exposing false propaganda that could harm U.S. interests.

While Middle East history in this century is drenched in blood, dominated by tyranny and scarred by the murder of millions of innocents, the causes of this massive injustice and inhumanity have failed to energize the American political left. Tragic, brutally violent conflicts in Iraq, Sudan, Syria and Yemen in the last 26 years have inspired no tent-cities, screaming protests, indignant op-eds or new categories of revolutionary study to university curricula.

Only one conflict has animated and energized the radical left as no other -- the Israeli-Palestinian conflict generally, and specifically, the Gaza war that Hamas started on Oct. 7, 2023. Ironically, the actual human and territorial impact of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict is dwarfed by the massive killing, destruction and savage cruelty caused by the region's other conflicts.

By most any measure of historical impact, the Israeli-Palestinian conflict would only rate a footnote. Why then has this conflict generated more attention among the political left -- as well as its handmaiden, the mainstream media -- than all the region's other conflicts combined?

Examining Israel's uniqueness in the Middle East, the reasons for its outsized attraction to the Western public, media, academics and radical-left activists seem obvious. Likewise, the reason that Israel has become a lightning rod for outraged criticism, condemnation and hate from the left is also explicable, given the left's revolutionary ideological roots.

As the Middle East's only liberal democracy, Israel certainly deserves attention from the West. Israel is also distinguished as the geographical and spiritual origin point of Christianity -- and, of course, Israel hosts significant religious sites for both Christians and Muslims. Furthermore, there's no ignoring that Israel is America's undisputed strongest ally in the region and among its most stalwart allies globally.

Finally, and above all, when assessing the disproportionate hostility toward Israel by the political left, we must note that Israel is the only non-Muslim country in the entire region -- a tiny outpost of just 10 million people on territory the size of New Jersey, dominated by a vast sea of half a billion Muslims, who occupy territory 550 times greater than the Jewish state.

Ironically, Israel's geographic and demographic underdog status buys it nothing from the ultraleft, which dogmatically categorizes the Jewish state's indigenous people as colonizing invaders and oppressors. Indeed, it is precisely the contrast between Israel's Jewish and Zionist values that makes it an enemy of today's neo-Marxists, who are increasingly poisoning American politics.

Volkswagen is selling its Osnabrück plant to an Israeli investment firm and to the German state of Lower Saxony. Instead of cars, the site is to build components for air defense systems, with Israel's state-owned Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, the maker of the Iron Dome, lined up as the anchor customer. The conversion is the most prominent case yet of Germany's struggling auto industry redirecting idle capacity into a booming defense sector.

Who Is Taking Over the Plant

Aurelius Capital, an investment firm based in Tel Aviv, will hold the majority stake in Volkswagen Osnabrück GmbH. The second shareholder will be Lower Saxony, which already owns about 20 percent of Volkswagen and is one of its largest investors. Volkswagen itself steps back as owner while pledging to support the transition with expertise and infrastructure. According to Volkswagen's statement, the plant is to become a "competence center for security and defense solutions." What has been signed so far is a letter of intent, and closing still depends on board approvals and regulatory clearance.

This Aurelius Capital is a separate company from the Munich-based investment group of the same name. The fund was founded by Alon Lifshitz and Tomer Jacob, both formerly of the Israeli venture firm Hanaco Ventures. Its team includes former NSA director Michael Rogers, former Israeli Air Force chief Amir Eshel and former Mossad deputy director Udi Lavi, The Jerusalem Post reported. The fund launched with 50 million US dollars and aims to grow to 150 million, investing in what it describes as "shields, not swords": cybersecurity, counter-drone technology and satellite systems. "Osnabrück brings with it something that cannot be built from scratch: many years of experience with demanding products, precise manufacturing processes and well-coordinated teams," Tomer Jacob said.

What Will Be Produced

The first joint venture between Aurelius, Lower Saxony and Rafael is an anchor project in air defense. Plans cover the manufacture of "systems and components for air defense systems for Germany and Europe." Early work is reported to center on carrier vehicles, launch systems and generators around the Iron Dome. Rafael chief executive Yoav Turgeman described the goal as a long-term industrial relationship "with the idea that the technology will be fully produced in Germany, to protect Germany and Europe." Further customers are expected to follow.

The timing is deliberate. Berlin plans to spend roughly 700 billion euros on defense over the next five years, and Rafael is separately hoping to sell the German government its Iron Dome system, which has a range of about 70 kilometers.

How the Qatar Conflict Is Being Sidestepped

A direct partnership between Volkswagen and Rafael had previously stalled against resistance from the Qatar Investment Authority, which holds about 17 percent of Volkswagen's voting rights and whose relationship with Israel has been strained since the autumn of 2023. Selling t
title: Volkswagen's Osnabrück Plant Set to Become an DefenseTech Factory for Israel's Rafael

The West Bank is an area of land located, as the name would suggest, on the west bank of the River Jordan.

Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 people since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem during the 1967 war.

An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.

Palestinians also want the land, along with Gaza, for a hoped-for future state.

Settlements are widely regarded as illegal under international law, and recent months have seen a rise in violence towards Palestinians in the West Bank by settlers.

Expansion has risen sharply since Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu's return to power in 2022, as well as the start of the Gaza war, triggered by Hamas's 7 October 2023 attack on Israel.
title: UK expected to announce sanctions on Israeli settlements in occupied West Bank

Susan Sarandon loses opportunities over her Gaza stance. On September 6, US actress Susan Sarandon was still having roles taken away from her in Hollywood because of her outspoken criticism of Israel's war in Gaza.

The "Thelma & Louise" star was dropped by her agency UTA in November 2023 over remarks at a pro-Palestinian rally, which she later said she regretted.

In an interview with the Venice Film Festival, where she has a role in the Italian film "The Echo Chamber", she claimed the "narrative" around the Gaza war and the United States' support for Israel had "completely changed". The Oscar winner told the press, referring to the extent of US financial and military aid for Israel, "There are a lot of things that people are aware of now".

She added, "I've still had movies taken away recently because there are agencies that are telling people not to hire me still. But that's the power structure".

I think there has been a change in terms of the understanding of the situation and the general public, but there are still very strongly held positions within my industry that are held by Zionists and who have not relaxed their feelings towards me.

She also added, "But I found my family, I found my people and I'm okay". The veteran star of "Dead Man Walking" has been one of Hollywood's most outspoken pro-Palestinian campaigners and critics of the Gaza war alongside others such as Marc Ruffalo, Richard Gere and Joaquin Phoenix. Many others have signed open letters criticising Israel's conduct of the war, which has left around 73,500 Palestinians dead and 174,500 injured since October 2023, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry.
title: Susan reveals she is losing movie roles over Gaza stance
author: Daily Times

content:
Oscar-winning actress discusses ongoing professional repercussions from her political activism

American actress Susan Sarandon has claimed she is still losing movie roles because of her outspoken support for Palestinians, nearly three years after she was dropped by talent agency UTA following controversial remarks at a pro-Palestinian rally.

The Oscar-winning actress, 79, made the claim at the Venice Film Festival while promoting her latest film, The Echo Chamber. Sarandon said movies had recently been 'taken away' from her and alleged that some agencies were continuing to discourage people from hiring her, despite what she sees as a broader shift in public attitudes towards Palestine.

Movies Are Still Being 'Taken Away'

Sarandon told reporters that her political activism continued to have professional consequences within the film industry.

'I've still had movies taken away recently because there are agencies that are telling people not to hire me still,' she said. 'But that's the power structure. I think [among] people, certainly internationally, I feel welcome.'

The Thelma & Louise star suggested the resistance was particularly pronounced when major Hollywood studios were involved.

'If it is a major studio, I think it's not just with me but with other people who have been told that that is impossible,' she said.

Sarandon did not identify the agencies, studios or film projects allegedly involved, and her claims have not been independently verified.

Why UTA Dropped Susan Sarandon in 2023

Sarandon was dropped by United Talent Agency in November 2023 after comments she made while attending a pro-Palestinian rally, weeks after the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October and the start of the war in Gaza.

'There are a lot of people afraid of being Jewish at this time, and are getting a taste of what it feels like to be a Muslim in this country,' Sarandon said at the time.

She later apologised, saying the wording was 'a terrible mistake' and acknowledging that it implied Jewish people had previously been strangers to persecution and discrimination.

Sarandon, who won the Academy Award for Best Actress for Dead Man Walking, has continued to speak publicly about Palestinians since the controversy.

Susan Sarandon Says Palestine Debate Has Shifted

At Venice, Sarandon argued that public understanding of Palestine, Israel and US policy had changed significantly since 2023.

'I think that the narrative has completely changed in terms of the historical relevance of Palestine and the ties of Zionists with America and our politics,' she said.

US opinion polling has documented shifting attitudes towards Israel and Palestinians during the Gaza war, although views vary considerably by political affiliation, age and other factors.

Sarandon contrasted those changes with what she described as continuing resistance within parts of Hollywood.

Palestine Debate Reaches Venice Film Festival

The Gaza war has also become an issue at this year's Venice Film
title: Susan Sarandon Claims Hollywood Is Still Punishing Her Over Palestine Support Nearly Three Years After UTA Split

Macklemore has responded to backlash over his "Free Palestine" comments at Ed Sheeran's concert. Here's what he said and why the rapper faces calls to leave the tour.

Macklemore has responded to the backlash over his calls to "Free Palestine" during his opening sets for Ed Sheeran's Loop Tour, saying his comments were about peace and equal rights and were not directed at Jewish people.

The rapper addressed the controversy on Monday, September 7, after facing criticism for using his performances at New Jersey's MetLife Stadium to speak about Palestine, Israel and other conflicts. He shared a video of his remarks on social media with the caption: "Wanting all humans to be treated equal should never be controversial."

The comments have also prompted a petition from the Israeli-American Council (IAC) calling for Macklemore to be removed from the remaining dates of Sheeran's US tour.

What did Macklemore say?

Macklemore used his set on September 5 to address the audience directly about Palestine before performing his 2024 protest song "Hind's Hall".

"One of the reasons why I wanted to come on this tour was because I wanted to stand up here on stages and stadiums across America and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: Free Palestine," he said.

He said he wanted people in Gaza and the occupied West Bank to know they had not been forgotten and thanked pro-Palestinian student protesters at Columbia University, Students for Justice in Palestine and Jewish Voice for Peace.

Macklemore also addressed Jewish members of the audience directly.

"To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters: criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you," he said. "My message is for peace; love for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect, and equality."

He then extended his message beyond Israel and Palestine, calling for freedom in Lebanon, Cuba, Congo and Sudan, as well as for people in the US who he said were living in fear of ICE.

Why is Macklemore facing backlash?

The remarks drew criticism from the Israeli-American Council, which launched a petition calling on Sheeran to remove Macklemore from the rest of the tour.

The organisation argued that the concert was "not a political rally, not a protest, and not an activist event", and questioned whether an opening act should use a major concert platform to promote what it described as a "one-sided political agenda".

The IAC's petition specifically objects to Macklemore's references to Israel, including his use of terms such as "apartheid" and "genocide". Those are political and contested characterisations, and the organisation's criticism reflects its position on Macklemore's remarks.

Macklemore, meanwhile, has rejected the suggestion that his criticism of Israeli policy amounts to criticism of Jewish people.

Macklemore says his message is about peace

In his response, Macklemore reiterated that his position is centred on equal treatmen
title: Macklemore responds to backlash over 'Free Palestine' comments at Ed Sheeran concert

content:
LONDON -- The UK government is to set out new restrictions on buying goods made in Jewish settlements in the occupied West Bank in what has been described as a broad reset of Britain's relations with Israel on Tuesday.

In an intervention that is expected to draw fierce criticism from the US and Israel, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband will announce a ban on the trade in goods and some services from the illegal Israeli settlements, promising the government will take a more active approach in supporting the Palestinian cause.

Miliband has also told civil society groups he is determined to reassert support for a two-state solution to the conflict with an appeal for the protection of Palestinian rights and respect for international law.

Miliband is expected to outline the measures in the Commons on Tuesday, which could include restrictions on trade in agricultural products from settlements.

Last week, Miliband said he would unveil a "comprehensive reset" of the British government's policy on Israel.

The Israeli government has previously warned it would retaliate if any new measures were introduced.

Settlements are illegal under international law, and recent months have seen a rise in violence towards Palestinians in the West Bank by settlers.

One minister told the BBC: "The statement will be a complete reset of the nature of our Israel-Palestine relationship. It will all feel very different.

"It is not just about sanctions. We hope that this will finally achieve what those of us who have been working towards for two years over the Middle East have been working on."

But Labour MPs briefed on the plans believe the sanctions will target trade with illegal settlements. They believe that means the sanctions would cover both goods and services.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham confirmed to Labour MPs at their weekly parliamentary meeting on Monday night that Miliband would be making the statement.

The prime minister is also said to have told the meeting that he had briefed international leaders about plans in phone calls on Monday afternoon.

Burnham spoke to US President Donald Trump over the phone on Monday, during which the prime minister stressed the importance of a two-state solution in the Middle East.

An official account of the call released by No 10 did not specify that Burnham had briefed Trump on the sanctions, while the US -- which is likely to strongly oppose the proposals -- has not commented.

Speaking in July, Stephen Doughty -- who was then Europe minister but has since been appointed Middle East minister -- told the business select committee that existing powers to impose restrictions on settlements did not go far enough.

Amid deficits from Chinese EVs, Volkswagen partners with Israeli defense firm to produce missile parts, reflecting Germany's shift to arms manufacturing

Volkswagen, Germany's national car brand, has decided to halt operations at its core vehicle assembly plant in the country and convert the facility into a defense industry site producing components for intercepting missiles. Volkswagen is struggling with its worst deficit since its founding, driven out of the market by low-cost Chinese electric vehicles. To overcome this, the company has partnered with an Israeli defense contractor to manufacture military equipment, a desperate measure to preserve local jobs and revenue. Experts assessed that even Germany, which has historically shunned war due to its experience in two world wars, has made a pragmatic judgment that producing weapons is more advantageous than building cars.

Volkswagen announced on the 7th (local time) that it had signed a letter of intent to sell its Osnabrück plant in northwestern Germany to the state of Lower Saxony and the Israeli investment firm Aurelius Capital. The sale price was not disclosed. Originally scheduled to end vehicle production in 2027, the plant will transform into a weapons production base once the sale process is finalized. However, even after becoming a defense factory, around 1,400 of the 1,800 workers who manufactured vehicles at the Osnabrück plant will retain their jobs. The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported that this is the first case of Volkswagen transferring an entire German factory to a defense facility.

Aurelius, which secured a majority stake in the plant, plans to collaborate with Rafael, Israel's state-owned defense company. Rafael led the design of Israel's air defense network, including the Iron Dome, which intercepts rockets and mortars, David's Sling, which blocks medium-range missiles, and Arrow, which neutralizes ballistic missiles in outer space. Volkswagen stated, "We plan to produce air defense systems and related components for Germany and Europe," adding, "This could open the way for further cooperation and follow-up projects."

Aurelius Capital told Reuters on the 7th, "The Osnabrück plant has long experience handling complex products, precise manufacturing processes, high-quality skilled labor, and a strong tradition." Olaf Lies, the Prime Minister of Lower Saxony, emphasized, "Fundamental changes have occurred in security situations and defense needs," urging, "Germany and Europe must strengthen manufacturing capabilities and become more independent."

Volkswagen, which is undergoing its largest restructuring in 89 years, approved the "Future Plan 2030" on the 4th of this month. The plan reduces production models by half and increases layoffs from the previously announced 50,000 people to 100,000 people. Four key assembly plants in Germany -- Emden, Zwickau, Hanover, and Neckarsulm, including Osnabrück -- are also under review for closure or repurposing. Oliver Blume, Volkswage
title: Volkswagen Converts Car Plant to Missile Component Production

JERUSALEM (VINnews) -- Adidas apologized Monday after an Israeli campaign featuring Shalev Biton, a former Israel Defense Forces soldier who lost a leg in a 2021 Hamas attack, drew boycott calls from anti-Israel activists.

The German sportswear company said an image used in "a recent local activation by the local team has raised concerns and strong reactions."

"It was never our intent to cause offense and we apologize for anyone affected," Adidas said in a statement issued from its global headquarters. "We acknowledge the concerns that have been raised and are taking the feedback seriously."

Biton was one of about 10 disabled athletes featured on posters in Adidas stores across Israel promoting the company's Single Shoe service, which allows customers with limb differences to buy one shoe at half the price of a pair rather than purchase a full set. The posters appeared only in Israel and were not part of Adidas's global campaign, which launched in Europe earlier this year.

Biton lost his left leg on May 12, 2021, while serving in the IDF's Nahal infantry brigade during Operation Guardian of the Walls. An anti-tank missile fired from Gaza struck the military vehicle he was in on the Israeli side of the border. His fellow soldier, Staff Sgt. Omer Tabib, was killed. Biton's leg later had to be amputated.

He has since learned to walk and run on a prosthetic limb, traveled abroad and proposed to his girlfriend. In 2025, Biton and a friend helped bring Israel's first youth participant to the European Amputee Football Federation Junior Camp in Romania.

Biton announced the Adidas collaboration on Instagram on Aug. 26, saying that after he returned to running he had been forced to buy full pairs of shoes even though he needed only one.

The Hebrew-language promotional video that circulated online made no mention of his military service or how he lost his leg. Critics nevertheless accused him of taking part in "genocide" and falsely claimed he was wounded in the current Gaza war, which began with the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, massacre in southern Israel. Spanish actor Javier Bardem was among those who amplified calls for a boycott.

In a post Monday, author and commentator Hen Mazzig said Adidas's apology "says everything."

"Meet the man Adidas felt the need to apologize for partnering with," Mazzig wrote, describing Biton's injury, recovery and advocacy. He noted Adidas's history as a company founded by Nazi Party members and said it was among the last major brands to cut ties with rapper Kanye West after his antisemitic remarks. Mazzig called the single-shoe program "a long-overdue correction" and said the company "never deserved to work with someone like Shalev."

Adidas said it would "continue to listen, learn and work to ensure that our actions reflect the inclusive values we stand for," and noted that the Single Shoe service is expanding across Europe, Asia and the Middle East, including the United Arab Emirates, the Palestinian territories, Leb
title: Adidas Apologizes For Featuring Israeli Veteran Who Lost Leg In Hamas Attack

Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis on Monday accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out airstrikes around the country, including the deadly bombardment of a prison, as the rebels press an offensive to seize territory near the Bab al-Mandab Strait.

The rebels' media said the attacks targeted Houthi positions across the Arabian Peninsula's poorest country, which is divided between areas held by the Iran-backed group and those controlled by the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government.

Saba news agency, which is affiliated with the Houthi movement, reported seven people were killed by Saudi airstrikes on the prison in Al-Hazm in the north of Yemen, including one child visiting the facility.

Seven others were wounded in the strikes on the prison, the agency added, citing the health ministry in the Houthi-held Yemeni capital of Sanaa. Footage shared by the rebel group of what they described as the damage to the prison located in Jawf province showed smoke rising from the blast site as rescue workers picked through rubble. Earlier, Sabaa reported "the Saudi enemy targeted the provinces of Jawf, Al-Bayda, Marib and Taiz with several airstrikes and cruise missiles."

Days of fighting near the Red Sea coast have left more than 300 people dead and displaced hundreds of families as the Houthis try to capture land bordering the Bab al-Mandab Strait.

Further footage shared by the Houthis showed what they said was the aftermath of a missile strike by the Iran-backed group on trucks carrying military equipment from Saudi Arabia to Al-Wadiah military camp in Yemen's Hadramawt province.

The Bab al-Mandab Strait forms the southern entrance to the Red Sea, a shipping artery that has become vital for Saudi oil exports amid Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz since the start of the US-Iran war.

The UN's special envoy for Yemen, Hans Grundberg, warned in a statement Monday that the Houthi assault had "triggered increasingly intense clashes, threatening to further expand the conflict."

"A return to sustained large-scale fighting will carry grave consequences for civilians and make an already difficult path toward a political settlement even harder," he added.

Military sources within the government forces also reported the air raids and missile attacks to Agence France-Presse. But Saudi Arabia did not announce any such strikes.

Most of the strikes were in Al-Bayda and Marib, targeting strategic positions, gatherings, and camps under Houthi control, the sources said on condition of anonymity.

On Saturday, a military official told AFP that Saudi airstrikes had targeted positions recently seized by the Houthis in Taiz governorate.

The Houthis and government forces have been fighting for days over control of Bab al-Mandab, marking the deadliest flare-up in Yemen since a 2022 ceasefire collapsed in July.

The Houthis, whose attacks seriously disrupted Red Sea shipping during the Gaza war, have also announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and have been targ
title: Yemen's Houthis accuse Saudi Arabia of air raids, missile strikes

The High Holidays traditionally bring prayer, charity and reflection.

This year, they bring heightened security.

Amid a spike in antisemitic incidents, Jewish communities around the country are preparing for one of their holiest periods by boosting security measures, such as surveillance systems, armed guards and trained volunteers to protect worshippers.

A surge in violent attacks has pushed anti-Jewish hate crimes to record highs. Last year, antisemitic incidents made up nearly 63% of all religion-motivated hate crimes nationwide, according to an analysis by the Anti-Defamation League.

Recent incidents in New Jersey demonstrate the danger posed to Jewish communities: In March, a young man leaving a Teaneck synagogue was shot with a gel pellet gun by a carload of teens who chased him and asked if he supported Israel or Palestine. In June, federal authorities charged a 22-year-old Wayne resident with planning an ISIS-inspired attack on a synagogue. Last month, Jewish organizations in Jackson Township were targeted in a series of antisemitic incidents.

Jewish leaders say the best response is not retreat but resilience and vigilance.

"Fear will not define us," said Jason Shames, CEO of the Jewish Federation of Northern New Jersey. "We are strong, connected and determined to live Jewishly, openly and proudly."

Rabbi Randall Mark of Congregation Shomrei Torah in Wayne said his synagogue, like many across the nation, has been forced to increase security measures in recent years, with cameras, armed guards and a volunteer security team.

"Sadly, security has become a major concern for synagogues in today's world," he said. "The challenge remains being welcoming to guests and at the same time protecting those who come to pray regularly. With the rise of antisemitism, it appears that this need is not going away anytime soon."

To achieve physical safety as well as peace of mind, congregants around the country are taking security into their own hands. In addition to using surveillance systems, metal detectors and armed guards, some synagogues are using their own volunteers as a security force.

One of the organizations seeing that demand firsthand is the Community Security Service, a New York-based nonprofit that provides free security training for Jewish organizations nationwide. The group deploys more than 7,100 volunteers who help protect roughly 500 synagogues and community events every week, said CEO Richard Priem. New organizations are joining the program weekly.

The CSS model combines trained volunteers with intelligence and guidance from law enforcement and community partners, such as the Anti-Defamation League.

Many houses of worship use the volunteers in addition to other security measures. It can be expensive for synagogues to foot the bill for a team of armed security guards, and federal grants provide limited funding. CSS volunteers have the additional advantage of being familiar with the membership and culture of their own synagogue
title: Rising antisemitism prompts tighter security at Jewish institutions

UK Pensions Minister Pat McFadden said the country will announce later today a trade ban on goods produced in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

"The foreign secretary will make a statement to Parliament later today," McFadden noted, Al Jazeera reported.

He said the measure reflects the UK's position, shared by many other countries, that the possibility of a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine should not be undermined.

The UK has adopted a tougher position on Israel since Prime Minister Andy Burnham took office in July.

Burnham has acknowledged the significance of the Israel-Palestine issue among Labour voters and, two months ago, apologised for the party's initial response to Israel's actions in Gaza, saying, "we got it wrong."
title: UK set to ban imports of goods from Israeli settlements in West Bank | News.az

Ed Miliband will announce a broad reset of the UK's relations with Israel on Tuesday, promising the government will take a more active approach in supporting the Palestinian cause.

In an intervention which has already drawn fierce criticism from the US and Israel, the foreign secretary will impose a UK ban on the trade in goods and some services from illegal Israeli settlements.

He has also told civil society groups he is determined to reassert support for a two-state solution to the conflict with an appeal for the protection of Palestinian rights and respect for international law.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, spoke to the US president, Donald Trump, on Monday night, a call which No 10 said "stressed the importance of a two-state solution" but gave no other details of the conversation.

On Tuesday the US ambassador to Israel said the US could issue its own reprisals against the UK. Mike Huckabee, who had claimed the Labour government was gripped by "Jew hatred", told BBC Radio 4's Today programme it would "do great damage to any Brits who are doing business in a number of states in the US".

He said he did not "know what all of the national sanctions or repercussions or retaliations will be from the US, it hasn't been announced yet ... but one of the largest US states, Florida, that has a law that if this action is taken, then Brits will not be able to do business with any company or business in Florida".

The work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, said on Tuesday that the motivation for the move was the desire to protect the viability of the two-state solution.

"At the heart of the statement is the idea that the UK, along with many other countries, do not want to see the possibility of a two-state solution in Israel and Palestine being erased by changes to the facts on the ground, and the reason that danger has become more urgent is because of expanded settlement activity in recent weeks and months," he told Sky News.

Plans in the so-called E1 area could mean the "effective cutting off of the north of the West Bank from the south of the West Bank", McFadden said. "But I think it's also important to say that Israel is an important trading partner for the UK. This isn't intended to be a boycott of all Israeli goods."

In his statement to MPs, Miliband is expected to use firmer language than his recent predecessors in calling out the humanitarian injustices suffered by Palestinians in Gaza.

The steps he lays out are likely to fall short of the full set of demands made by Palestinian advocacy groups, but they will still be seen as a sign that the UK is moving beyond traditional rhetorical support for a two-state solution towards active steps to forestall the expansion of illegal settlements in the West Bank - widely seen as intended to destroy the prospect of a Palestinian state.

Britain will announce a trade ban on goods made in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank later on Tuesday, confirmed a senior minister, as part of the UK's efforts to support a two-state solution.

Six weeks into his new job, foreign minister Ed Miliband flagged last week that he was looking at resetting Britain's policy on Israel, and he is due to make a statement on Israel and trading restrictions in the House of Commons.

For the latest updates on the Israel-Palestine conflict, visit our dedicated page.

Britain's new Prime Minister Andy Burnham, also in office since July, spoke to U.S. President Donald Trump on Monday to stress the "the importance of the two-state solution", in what is seen as a reference to the sanctions.

Miliband said last week that Israel's E1 settlement project in the West Bank would cut across land which the Palestinians seek for a state, putting at risk the two-state solution.

Asked about how the trade ban would operate, pensions minister Pat McFadden did not give details.

"The foreign secretary will make a statement to Parliament later today," McFadden told Times Radio.

"The reason that danger has become more urgent is because of expanded settlement activity in recent weeks and months."

UN bodies and most governments, including Britain, consider Israeli settlements in the West Bank illegal under international law, and regard the West Bank as territory under Israeli military occupation.

Israel argues that the territory is disputed rather than occupied, and asserts that Jews have a historical right to the land.

The Israeli prime minister's office and the foreign ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

content:
When Fauda Season 4 ended an eternity and a devastating war ago, our hero was at death's door, reciting both the central prayer of Judaism, the Shema, and the Muslim Fatiha.

It was a cliffhanger with monumental implications for Doron Kavillio (Lior Raz), an Israeli Jew who spent his days undercover as a Muslim Arab -- an identity crisis long in coming. Zoom out and you can see the doomed duality of Israel and Palestine, Jew and Muslim, connected in a cycle of death and more alike than they may seem.

Season 5 begins bilingually, with Hebrew and Arab definitions of the Arabic word Tha'r, blood revenge, "restoring violated honor or avenging injustice." This concept is now the point of commonality -- not how men pray, but how they seek revenge.

Welcome to a post-Oct. 7 Israel. Doron is in therapy, struggling to recall eight missing hours of his life on the day of Hamas' attack on the Gaza envelope.

Comrades have left the country -- Steve (Doron Ben-David) is protecting oligarchs in London, Sagi and Nurit are in Australia. Eli (Yaakov Zada-Daniel) is now Orthodox, living in a settlement and reeling from the murder of his wife and stepchildren at his now-torched kibbutz. When a Bedouin friend, Salem (Bian Anteer) who lost his son in the raid on Eli's home, approaches him with a tip on the Nukhba fighter responsible, they depart for Marseille to answer the call of Tha'r.

It would hardly be Fauda if this act of vengeance didn't give way to a much larger plot. Marseille is the staging ground for Saeed el Hatib (French-Algerian actor Hakim Djaziri), "the Sinwar of Europe," who is recruiting sympathetic, white continentals for a fresh massacre in Israel.

Fauda has always made some viewers uncomfortable. Massively entertaining, bingeable to those of us who stream it in the Netflix aftermarket, its existence was premised on ongoing injustices in the West Bank and Gaza and the violence that bursts through their borders. (The BDS movement labelled it a "war-crimes glorifying" series;" Haaretz called it "morally dubious.")

And yet as late as the last season it contained very real criticism of Israel's conduct, including its costly campaigns to recover captured soldiers and the torture used to extract information on their whereabouts. The show always alluded to real operations -- Cast Lead, Brother's Keeper -- in dialogue. But because it can't merely mention an attack as raw and monumental as Oct. 7, and because it has no desire to question the response to it, it chooses to recreate its savagery.

Episodes 7 and 8, flashbacks to that day, are front-loaded with a trigger warning and a disclaimer that you can skip them and still be able to follow the main plot.

It's hard for me to recommend those episodes. If not exactly atrocity porn, their central, race-against-time set piece is too anchored in recent events and constructed too much like an action movie. It feels in a sense exploitative, even if intended as a tribute. (To give them credit, both Lior Raz a
title: In new 'Fauda' season, the aftershocks of Oct. 7, without a thought for Gaza

* Calls to expel UK Ambassador to Israel Simon Walters

* Bezalel Smotrich says UK has 'antisemitic government'

DUBAI: Israel's Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich has called for the immediate expulsion of the UK Ambassador to Israel Simon Walters, amid speculation that Britain would institute sanctions on Israel.

Israeli media has reported that the UK would likely impose a new set of sanctions on Israel including a ban on products from illegal settlements in occupied territories in the West Bank.

In a post on X, Smotrich said Israel would not be a "doormat" to what he called the "antisemitic" government of the UK.

"Expel the British ambassador tonight! We will not be a doormat trampled by an antisemitic government, in a country conquered by radical Islam, trying to save itself from economic and social decline by attacking Jews and the state of Israel," he said.

"The British mandate in the land of Israel is over," added Smotrich.

Meanwhile, Israel's National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir urged Israel to recognize Argentine sovereignty over the Falkland Islands which are administered by Britain, but claimed by Argentina.

"It is time for the state of Israel to officially recognize that the Falkland Islands are occupied Argentine territory, stolen by the British by force from the Argentine people," said Ben-Gvir.

Ben-Gvir also claimed that the UK government was exploiting oil resources around the Falkland Islands.

The UK is set to announce a series of new sanctions imposed on Israel on Tuesday, according to Secretary of State for Work and Pensions Pat McFadden.

"The foreign secretary ⁠will make a statement to Parliament later today, and at the ⁠heart of the statement is the idea that the UK, along with many other countries, do not want to see the possibility of a two-state ⁠solution ⁠in Israel and Palestine being erased," said McFadden.
title: Israeli ministers seek retaliation over expected UK sanctions

Adidas Arabia apologises for campaign backlash amid tensions in the Israel-Palestine conflict

Adidas Arabia apologised after a local Single Shoe campaign featuring a former Israeli soldier and amputee sparked backlash. 'We recognize that an image used in a recent local activation has raised concerns and strong reactions,' a statement posted on Adidas Arabia read. It was posted in both Arabic and English.

'It was never our intent to cause offence, and we apologise to anyone affected. We acknowledge the concerns that have been raised and are taking feedback seriously. Inclusion is a core value at Adidas, and we remain committed to expanding access to sport,' the statement continued.

Single-Shoe Service

The controversy began with an Adidas campaign in Israel featuring 11 athletes with disabilities, including Shalev Biton, a former member of the IDF (Israel Defense Forces). Biton's left leg was amputated after he suffered wounds in 2021 while serving in the Israeli army.

The service allows eligible customers with limb differences to buy a single shoe for 50% of the price of a full pair. Pro-Palestinian activists criticised the campaign and showed videos of the many Palestinians, especially children, who also lost their limbs in Israel's continued war on Gaza.

UNRWA Commissioner-General Philippe Lazzarini said in December 2025 that Gaza had become home to the largest group of child amputees in modern history. A 2025 WHO publication said more than 10 children in Gaza were losing one or both legs each day.

In an August 2025 UN committee session, Ibrahim Khraishi, the Palestinian permanent observer to the UN Office at Geneva, said 4,800 limb amputations had been documented since the start of the war, with 76% involving upper limbs and 24% lower limbs.

'Our Single-Shoe service (is) designed to better serve people for whom a traditional pair of shoes may not reflect their needs,' Adidas also said in its statement. The service was launched in Europe early this year, and will soon expand across Asia and countries in the Middle East: Egypt, Kuwait, Lebanon, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, United Arab Emirates and Palestine.

Adidas's Past Controversies

The German brand has sought to remain neutral in the Israel-Palestine conflict, yet controversies have repeatedly drawn it into the debate.

In 2012, several Arab nations called for a boycott of the brand following its sponsorship of the Jerusalem Marathon. The route passed through parts of East Jerusalem, whose status is disputed and widely regarded by the international community as occupied Palestinian territory. The sponsorship put Adidas among the companies targeted by boycott campaigns.

In 2018, around 130 Palestinian football clubs and sports associations urged Adidas to end its sponsorship of the Israel Football Association, arguing that some of the clubs in the Israeli federation are in disputed West Bank territory. Adidas initially resisted, saying it operates in a 'politically neutral way.' The deal la

A Palestinian man was shot dead when Israeli forces surrounded a house and opened fire during an early-morning military incursion into Aqraba, south of Nablus in the occupied West Bank, Palestinian media reported on Tuesday.

Local sources claimed that Israeli forces surrounded a house in the al- Dairiya neighborhood and ordered a man inside to surrender, threatening to blow up the house if he refused. But the man didn't give up, the reports said.

Witnesses reported sustained gunfire and at least two explosions coming from inside or around the house. Later, Israeli forces brought a military bulldozer to the area and fired an Energa projectile at the building, the Palestinian news agency WAFA reported.

Palestinian media later identified the man as Abdul Karim Bani Jaber, saying he was shot dead during the operation.

The Israeli military had not yet issued a statement confirming the circumstances of the killing.

Adidas has apologised following backlash and boycott calls over a local advertising campaign in Israel promoting its "Single Shoe" service, which featured a former Israeli soldier who lost his left leg after being wounded while serving in the military.

The campaign featured Shalev Biton, whose left leg was amputated after he was wounded in 2021. Adidas' "Single Shoe" initiative allows people with limb differences to buy an individual shoe for 50% of the price of a pair, says Andalou Ajansi.

The campaign drew criticism from pro-Palestinian activists and high-profile figures, including Spanish actor Javier Bardem, who objected to the decision to feature a former Israeli soldier in an advertising campaign focused on amputees.

Critics also pointed to the thousands of Palestinians who have lost limbs during the war in Gaza. The World Health Organization estimated in May that more than 5,000 traumatic limb amputations had occurred in Gaza since October 2023.

Adidas apologised in response to the backlash, saying the posters were a "local activation" rather than a global campaign. The company said it never intended to cause offence.

The controversy is the latest involving Adidas and its activities connected to Israel and Palestine over the past 15 years.

Jerusalem Marathon

In 2012, Adidas faced boycott calls from Arab sports officials over its sponsorship of the Jerusalem Marathon, whose route crossed through Occupied East Jerusalem.

The company was no longer a sponsor of the event the following year.

Israel Football Association sponsorship

In 2018, more than 130 Palestinian football clubs and sports associations called on Adidas to end its sponsorship of the Israel Football Association (IFA), citing the inclusion of clubs based in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank.

Adidas eventually ended its sponsorship of the association, although it did not publicly link the decision to the campaign.

Bella Hadid shoe campaign

In 2024, Adidas faced a major social media backlash and boycott calls after removing Palestinian-American model Bella Hadid from a retro shoe campaign tied to the 1972 Munich Olympics, following criticism from Israel.

Adidas later apologised for what it called an "unintentional mistake", but did not reinstate Hadid.
title: Adidas apologises after Israel ad campaign sparks backlash
author: The Business Standard

With Andy Burnham's government preparing to unveil sanctions against Israel, the pro-Palestinian lobby and the left more broadly has grounds for celebration. This is a victory for their anti-Zionist worldview. The pretext for the sanctions is Israeli settlement-building, something the British government has consistently condemned, but the context is a highly effective (and handsomely funded) campaign since October 7 to demonise Israel so thoroughly in the minds of Western populations that many formerly sympathetic to the Jewish state would turned sceptical, if not hostile, as some have in recent times.

Some of that is an organic process. Israel's errors military and diplomatic have alienated long-term friends, as has the presence around the cabinet table of Itamar Ben Gvir, a loudmouthed simpleton, and Bezalel Smotrich, a dangerous fanatic. But much of it is the result of a propaganda war funded by Qatar and Iran, Islamic states suspiciously eager to separate Western nations from a country known for its advanced defence technology, unparalleled intelligence, and expertise in identifying and breaking up Islamist terror cells. The frustration you feel towards Israel might well be sincere, but ask yourself why Islamic regimes are so keen for you to feel that way.

The answer matters because, while the government's Palestine pivot is largely motivated by domestic concerns, the campaign to bring it about was orchestrated overseas with the aim of driving a wedge between Israel and the West. This campaign understood British society and politics very well. Amplify genuine civilian suffering in Gaza, mix in a whole lot of falsehoods, distortions and propaganda, and Britons across the board would soon shed whatever sympathy they felt for Israel after October 7. For the bulk of British voters, however, this was as far as they could be taken; Palestine is simply not a big issue for them. But there was a demographic with insatiable appetites for a diet of Jewish perfidy in Muslim lands, as the results of the 2024 election showed.

Labour looks at its heartlands across urban England, in London, Birmingham, Leeds, and elsewhere, and is alarmed by what it sees. Seats like Yardley (Jess Phillips), Ilford North (Wes Streeting), and Bradford West (Naz Shah) which came breathtakingly close to voting for Gaza-focused candidates in 2024. Seats like Birmingham Ladywood (Shabana Mahmood), Slough (Tan Dhesi), and Rochdale (Paul Waugh), where independents or the Workers Party of Britain (WPB) came with ten per cent of toppling a Labour MP. Seats like Birmingham Hodge Hill and Solihull North (Liam Byrne), Bethnal Green and Stepney (Rushanara Ali), and Dudley (Sonia Kumar), where modest increases in support for the Greens, the WPB (Workers Party of Britain) and Palestinianist independents could be enough to cost Labour candidates victory next time.
